title: How to Fail at AI Strategy: Hamel Husain & Greg Ceccarelli

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core subject is human and organizational factors in AI: executive-practitioner disconnects, jargon excluding domain experts, trust in AI outputs, and the need for human-in-the-loop data review. Advice applies cross-domain to any organization, while the organizational and enterprise-workflow framing maps to enterprise operations. Covers strategy planning via silo creation and fake diagnosis, evaluation via metric hoarding and data avoidance, and deployment via untested production launches. The satirical, non-technical framing is accessible to both executives and practitioners without ML expertise. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer Summit 2025 Leadership Track. Claims rest on the speakers' direct experience helping 30+ companies but lack formal research methodology or quantitative validation.

summary: Hamel Husain (ML engineer/consultant) and Greg Ceccarelli (executive leader/AI startup co-founder) present a satirical 'worse practices' guide to AI strategy failure, built on Charlie Munger's 'invert always invert' principle. Having collectively interacted with 30+ companies, they structure their advice as sequential steps toward guaranteed disaster. Step 1: Divide and conquer your own company by creating impenetrable silos between teams, attending AI conferences without sharing learnings, and embracing the 'anti-value stick'—where WTP becomes 'Wishful Thinking Promises,' PRICE becomes 'Particularly Ridiculous Infrastructure Costs Everywhere,' COST represents cascading technical debt, and WTS is simply 'because AI.' Step 2: Fake any diagnosis by highlighting random paragraphs from annual reports without consulting practitioners. Adopt vague guiding policies like 'become the global AI leader in everything.' Embrace perpetual beta and bury teams under 4,000-page documents. For communication, use jargon strategically to obfuscate jobs-to-be-done—replacing 'write a prompt' with 'building agents' to exclude domain experts. Hamel shares a mental health client example where this jargon kept subject-matter experts out of the room. For mobilization, use 'zoning to lose'—randomly assigning AI tasks to inexperienced people and launching untested chatbots directly to production. Throw tools at problems without root-cause analysis, treat evals as a vendor problem, hoard every off-the-shelf metric, optimize for cosine similarity and BLEU/ROUGE without checking user experience, and never cross-check with domain experts. The ultimate technique: avoid looking at data entirely—trust AI outputs without inspection, rely on gut feelings for million-dollar decisions, dismiss simple annotation tools like spreadsheets, and make data inaccessible by requiring custom PhD-operated platforms. The talk concludes with a wrap-up of the foolproof failure guide and points to real resources at ai-exec and an upcoming O'Reilly book, noting that while the talk was inverted, their lived experience and willingness to help is genuine.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Invert your thinking—studying how to guarantee failure reveals what success requires
Organizational silos between executives and practitioners are a primary cause of AI project failure
Overpromising AI capabilities without practical grounding creates unrealistic expectations and technical debt
Jargon strategically excludes domain experts from AI development, degrading solution quality
Throwing tools at problems without root-cause analysis wastes resources and perpetuates failure
Off-the-shelf evaluation metrics that don't track business outcomes provide false confidence
Avoiding data inspection and relying on gut feelings blinds teams to actual failure modes
Making data inaccessible through complex systems prevents domain experts from contributing
Simple tools like spreadsheets and Airtable are often sufficient for data annotation and review
Real, non-inverted guidance is available through their ai-exec resource and upcoming O'Reilly book

sections.title: Introduction and Inversion Framing
sections.summary: Greg and Hamel introduce themselves as an executive leader and ML engineer respectively, framing the talk around Charlie Munger's 'invert always invert' principle. They position themselves as a 'dream team of disaster' who have witnessed numerous AI strategy failures across companies.

sections.title: Step 1: Divide and Conquer Your Company
sections.summary: The first failure step is creating organizational silos and disconnects. They introduce the 'anti-value stick' framework: WTP becomes Wishful Thinking Promises (promise AI does everything), PRICE becomes Particularly Ridiculous Infrastructure Costs Everywhere (buy expensive GPUs without cost-benefit analysis), COST represents cascading technical debt, and WTS is simply 'because AI' with no further explanation needed.

sections.title: Step 2: Define Strategy Through Fake Diagnosis
sections.summary: Failure step two involves faking strategic diagnosis by highlighting random paragraphs from annual reports without consulting practitioners. Guiding policy should be vague ('become the global AI leader in everything'), action plans should be buzzword-driven (AI SEO, generative art NFTs, drone lunch delivery), and timelines should be replaced with perpetual beta and massive GitHub backlogs.

sections.title: Communication Through Jargon Obfuscation
sections.summary: Jargon should be used strategically to hide jobs-to-be-done and exclude domain experts. Hamel shares a mental health client example where saying 'building agents' instead of 'writing a prompt' kept experts out of the room. Greg parallels this by using 'RAG' instead of 'ensuring AI context' and 'prompt injections' instead of 'users tricking AI.' Engineers should write prompts instead of customer experts.

sections.title: Mobilization: Zoning to Lose
sections.summary: The 'zoning to lose' framework involves randomly assigning AI tasks to people with no relevant experience, outsourcing data review to offshore teams lacking business context, and launching untested, bug-ridden chatbots directly to production without quality assurance or beta testing, risking career-ending PR disasters.

sections.title: Tools Not Processes and Metric Hoarding
sections.summary: Instead of analyzing problems, throw tools at them—buy expensive vector databases when retrieval fails, fine-tune without measurement, treat evals as a vendor problem. Create dashboards hoarding every off-the-shelf metric, optimize for cosine similarity and BLEU/ROUGE, never cross-check with domain experts or users, and keep hoarding metrics until one goes up-and-to-the-right to claim success.

sections.title: Avoid Looking at Data
sections.summary: The most potent failure technique is introduced: avoid looking at data entirely. Keep a blindfold on at all times. This sets up the transition to deeper exploration of data avoidance strategies.

sections.title: Data Inaccessibility and Conclusion
sections.summary: The data avoidance theme deepens: leaders should trust AI outputs without inspection, rely on gut feelings for million-dollar decisions, and dismiss simple annotation tools like spreadsheets as 'beneath them.' Critical advice is to make data inaccessible by insisting on custom PhD-operated platforms instead of simple tools like Airtable, ensuring domain experts cannot contribute. The talk wraps up as a 'foolproof guide in under 20 minutes to achieving total AI failure.' Hamel and Greg reveal their real resources: the ai-exec website and an upcoming O'Reilly book (February 27th), emphasizing that while the talk was inverted, their lived experience is genuine and they are eager to help.
